note.explanation: Biomolecules are important molecules in living things. Carbohydrates mainly provide energy, proteins have many roles including growth and repair, lipids store energy and form membranes, and nucleic acids store and use genetic information. Water is the medium in which many of these processes occur.
examples: Glucose is a monosaccharide used in respiration to release energy.
DNA stores genetic information; RNA helps use that information to make proteins.
note.checkAnswer: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine; DNA contains thymine instead of uracil.
note.simple: Living things contain different kinds of molecules. Each kind has a particular job, such as providing energy, building structures, or carrying instructions.
note.checkQuestion: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
note.title: Biomolecules: the main ideas
steps: Carbohydrates include sugars and starches; they are a major energy source.
Proteins are made from amino acids and perform many structural and functional jobs.
Most lipids are made from fatty acids and glycerol; they store energy and help form cell membranes.
DNA stores inherited information. RNA helps use that information to make proteins.
Water dissolves many substances and provides a medium for reactions in cells.
note.answer: Biomolecules are molecules in living things, including carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

mcqs.stem: Q6.1. What is the primary function of carbohydrates?
rationales: Correct: carbohydrates are a major source of energy for the body.
Incorrect: some proteins act as enzymes; carbohydrates are not primarily enzymes.
Incorrect: regulation is not the primary function of carbohydrates.
Incorrect: lipids and proteins are important membrane components, not the primary function of carbohydrates.

options: Monosaccharides are present in plant cell wall.
mcqs.stem: Q6.2. How will you differentiate between monosaccharides and polysaccharides?
rationales: Correct: a monosaccharide is a single sugar unit, whereas a polysaccharide has many sugar units.
Incorrect: polysaccharides are generally not sweet.
Incorrect: plant cell walls contain the polysaccharide cellulose.
Incorrect: polysaccharides generally do not dissolve easily in water.

options: It is digestible by human digestive system.
It provides structural support in plants.
mcqs.stem: Q6.3. What is true about cellulose?
rationales: Incorrect: cellulose is not sweet.
Incorrect: humans cannot digest cellulose because they lack the enzyme to break it down.
Correct: cellulose strengthens plant cell walls and provides structural support.
Incorrect: cellulose is insoluble in water.

mcqs.stem: Q6.4. Which of the following proteins is involved in oxygen transport?
rationales: Incorrect: insulin is a hormone that helps regulate blood glucose.
Correct: haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen.
Incorrect: collagen is a structural protein in connective tissues.
Incorrect: keratin is a structural protein found in hair, nails and skin.

mcqs.stem: Q6.5. Which component of an amino acid determines its unique properties?
rationales: Incorrect: the amino group is common to amino acids and does not distinguish their properties.
Incorrect: the carboxyl group is common to amino acids and does not distinguish their properties.
Correct: the variable R group gives each amino acid its distinctive properties.
Incorrect: hydrogen is not the variable group that distinguishes amino acids.

mcqs.stem: Q6.6. Which proteins are involved in defence against pathogens?
rationales: Correct: antibodies bind to particular foreign substances and help defend the body.
Incorrect: myosin is involved in muscle contraction.
Incorrect: fibrinogen helps blood clot.
Incorrect: haemoglobin transports oxygen.

mcqs.stem: Q6.7. Which of the following are the units of most lipids?
rationales: Incorrect: amino acids are the building units of proteins.
Correct: many lipids, including fats and oils, are made from fatty acids and glycerol.
Incorrect: nucleotides are the building units of nucleic acids.
Incorrect: simple sugars are building units of carbohydrates.

options: They contain double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.
They are solid at room temperature.
They are found only in animal fats.
mcqs.stem: Q6.8. How do unsaturated fatty acids differ from saturated fatty acids?
rationales: Incorrect: unsaturated fatty acids have fewer hydrogen atoms than the corresponding saturated fatty acids because of double bonds.
Correct: unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.
Incorrect: unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature.
Incorrect: unsaturated fatty acids are found in plant oils and some animal fats, not only in animal fats.

mcqs.stem: Q6.9. Which of the following is NOT a function of proteins?
rationales: Incorrect: haemoglobin is a protein that transports oxygen in blood.
Correct: DNA and RNA, which are nucleic acids, carry genetic information.
Incorrect: digestive enzymes are proteins that help digest food.
Incorrect: antibodies are proteins that help defend against pathogens.

mcqs.stem: Q6.10. Which components make up a nucleotide?
rationales: Correct: a nucleotide consists of a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
Incorrect: amino acids are not components of a nucleotide.
Incorrect: fatty acids are not components of a nucleotide.
Incorrect: proteins are not components of a nucleotide.

mcqs.stem: Q6.11. Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
rationales: Incorrect: adenine is found in both DNA and RNA.
Incorrect: thymine is found in DNA; RNA uses uracil instead.
Correct: uracil occurs in RNA in place of thymine.
Incorrect: guanine is found in both DNA and RNA.

written.text: Q6.1. What are the main functions of carbohydrates in the body?
written.finalAnswer: Carbohydrates provide energy, store energy and can form structural materials.

rubric.why: The main role of carbohydrates is providing energy.
rubric.how: Mention energy as a main function.

rubric.why: Carbohydrates also have storage or structural roles.
rubric.description: Give a further function of carbohydrates.
rubric.how: Mention energy storage, or a structural role such as cellulose.

modelAnswer: Carbohydrates are a major source of energy for the body.
They can also store energy and form structural materials.

written.text: Q6.2. How do the three group of carbohydrates differ in taste?
written.finalAnswer: Monosaccharides and disaccharides are sweet; polysaccharides are generally not sweet.

rubric.why: The simple sugar groups are sweet in taste.
rubric.description: State the taste of monosaccharides and disaccharides.
rubric.how: Say that monosaccharides and disaccharides taste sweet.

rubric.why: Polysaccharides differ from the simple sugars in taste.
rubric.how: Say they are generally not sweet or tasteless.

modelAnswer: Monosaccharides and disaccharides are sweet in taste.
Polysaccharides are generally not sweet.

written.text: Q6.3. Name two common monosaccharides and two disaccharides.
written.finalAnswer: Monosaccharides: glucose and fructose. Disaccharides: sucrose and maltose.

rubric.why: The answer needs two examples of monosaccharides.
rubric.how: Give any two correct examples, such as glucose and fructose.

rubric.why: The answer needs two examples of disaccharides.
rubric.how: Give any two correct examples, such as sucrose and maltose.

modelAnswer: Two common monosaccharides are glucose and fructose.
Two common disaccharides are sucrose and maltose.

written.text: Q6.4. Which monosaccharides make a sucrose molecule?

rubric.why: One monosaccharide in sucrose is glucose.
rubric.how: Include glucose in the answer.

rubric.why: Sucrose is made from glucose and fructose together.
rubric.description: Name fructose as the other monosaccharide.
rubric.how: Give both glucose and fructose.

modelAnswer: A sucrose molecule is made up of glucose and fructose.

written.text: Q6.5. Give an example of a storage polysaccharide in plants.

rubric.why: Starch is the storage polysaccharide in plants.
rubric.how: Answer starch.

modelAnswer: Starch is a storage polysaccharide in plants.

written.text: Q6.6. Define amino acid and draw its structure.
written.finalAnswer: An amino acid is an organic molecule with an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group attached to a central carbon.

rubric.why: An amino acid has both an amino group and a carboxyl group.
rubric.description: Define an amino acid by its characteristic groups.
rubric.how: Identify the amino and carboxyl groups.

rubric.why: The general structure shows the groups and variable side group attached to the central carbon.
rubric.description: Draw or describe the general structure.
rubric.how: Show a central carbon bonded to H, R, NH₂ and COOH.

modelAnswer: An amino acid is an organic molecule that has an amino group (–NH₂) and a carboxyl group (–COOH).
General structure:      H
H₂N—C—COOH
R

written.text: Q6.7. What are the basic components of lipids? Draw their structures.
written.finalAnswer: Many lipids are made of glycerol and fatty acids; a fat molecule has one glycerol joined to three fatty acids.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the basic components of many lipids.
rubric.how: State glycerol and fatty acids.

rubric.why: The structure of a fat shows how the components are joined.
rubric.description: Draw or describe a fat structure.
rubric.how: Show one glycerol joined to three fatty acid chains.

modelAnswer: Many lipids are made from glycerol and fatty acids.
A fat molecule has one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acid molecules.
Structure: glycerol — (fatty acid)₃

written.text: Q6.8. What are the types of RNA? Write their functions.
written.finalAnswer: The three main types are messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

rubric.why: The response should identify the three main types of RNA.
rubric.description: Name the three types of RNA.
rubric.how: Give mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.

rubric.why: Each RNA type has a role in protein synthesis.
rubric.how: Explain that mRNA carries the code, tRNA brings amino acids and rRNA forms part of ribosomes.

modelAnswer: Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries genetic instructions from DNA to the ribosome.
Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries amino acids to the ribosome.
Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) forms part of the ribosome and helps in protein synthesis.

written.text: Q6.9. Briefly describe the function of DNA.
written.finalAnswer: DNA stores hereditary information and provides instructions for making proteins.

rubric.why: DNA's key role is storing inherited information.
rubric.description: State that DNA stores hereditary information.
rubric.how: Use the terms genetic or hereditary information.

rubric.why: DNA information directs cell activities, including protein production.
rubric.description: Explain what the information is used for.
rubric.how: Mention that it provides instructions for making proteins.

modelAnswer: DNA stores hereditary information in its sequence of bases.
It provides instructions for making proteins and directing cell activities.

written.text: Q6.1. Write a comprehensive note on the structures and roles of the three classes of carbohydrates.
written.finalAnswer: Monosaccharides are single sugar units; disaccharides contain two joined monosaccharides; polysaccharides contain many joined monosaccharides. Carbohydrates provide energy, store energy and have structural roles.

rubric.why: The structure of the first class must be distinguished.
rubric.how: State that they are single sugar units and give an example.

rubric.why: Disaccharides are made from two joined monosaccharides.
rubric.how: State that two monosaccharides are joined; examples include sucrose and maltose.

rubric.why: Polysaccharides consist of many sugar units.
rubric.how: State that many monosaccharides form a polysaccharide; examples include starch and cellulose.

rubric.why: Carbohydrates are an important energy source.
rubric.how: Mention energy release in respiration.

rubric.why: Storage and structural roles complete the account of carbohydrate roles.
rubric.how: Mention starch or glycogen storage and cellulose's structural role.

modelAnswer: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Monosaccharides are single sugar units; examples include glucose and fructose.
Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join; examples include sucrose and maltose.
Polysaccharides are long chains of many monosaccharides; examples include starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Carbohydrates provide energy for cellular activities, and glucose is used in respiration.
Starch in plants and glycogen in animals store energy.
Cellulose forms plant cell walls and provides structural support.

written.text: Q6.2. Discuss the functions of proteins.
written.finalAnswer: Proteins provide structure, act as enzymes and hormones, transport substances, enable movement, defend against pathogens and help blood clot.

rubric.why: Proteins build and repair body structures.
rubric.description: State a structural or growth-and-repair role.
rubric.how: Give examples such as collagen or keratin, or mention growth and repair.

rubric.why: Many proteins catalyse reactions, including digestion.
rubric.how: Mention enzymes and their role in speeding reactions.

rubric.why: Some proteins transport substances around the body.
rubric.how: Give haemoglobin transporting oxygen as an example.

rubric.why: Proteins help protect the body from pathogens.
rubric.how: Mention antibodies or defence against pathogens.

rubric.why: Other roles show the range of protein functions.
rubric.how: Mention movement, clotting or hormonal regulation.

modelAnswer: Proteins are needed for growth and repair and form structural materials such as collagen and keratin.
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, including digestion.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Antibodies help defend the body against pathogens.
Proteins also take part in movement, blood clotting and regulation; for example, myosin works in muscle and insulin is a protein hormone.

written.text: Q6.3. What are fatty acids? Explain their types.
written.finalAnswer: Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon-chain molecules with a carboxyl group. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.

rubric.why: This describes the basic chemical structure of a fatty acid.
rubric.how: Describe a hydrocarbon chain with a carboxyl group.

rubric.why: Saturated fatty acids are identified by having no carbon–carbon double bonds.
rubric.how: State that their carbon chain has no double bonds.

rubric.why: Double bonds distinguish unsaturated fatty acids.
rubric.how: State that they have one or more carbon–carbon double bonds.

rubric.why: Unsaturated fatty acids can be further classified by the number of double bonds.
rubric.how: Distinguish monounsaturated (one) from polyunsaturated (more than one).

rubric.why: A characteristic property or source helps compare the types.
rubric.description: Give a valid comparison or example.
rubric.how: For example, unsaturated oils are often liquid at room temperature; saturated fats are often solid.

modelAnswer: Fatty acids are molecules with a long hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl group (–COOH).
Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains; they contain the maximum number of hydrogen atoms.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more carbon–carbon double bonds.
A fatty acid with one double bond is monounsaturated; one with more than one is polyunsaturated.
Unsaturated fats are often liquid at room temperature, while saturated fats are often solid.

written.text: Q6.4. Describe the basic structure of fats and oils. Explain how lipids play role in energy storage.
written.finalAnswer: A fat or oil molecule is generally a triglyceride: one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids. Lipids store energy in their chemical bonds and provide a long-term energy reserve.

rubric.why: A triglyceride's components must be correctly identified.
rubric.how: State one glycerol joined to three fatty acids.

rubric.why: The components must be described as chemically connected.
rubric.description: Explain how the components are linked.
rubric.how: Mention that glycerol and fatty acids are joined by bonds.

rubric.why: Lipids contain energy that can be released when needed.
rubric.how: State that energy is stored in lipid molecules.

rubric.why: This completes the explanation of lipids as an energy store.
rubric.description: Describe the storage advantage or role.
rubric.how: Mention long-term energy reserve or that lipids store more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

modelAnswer: Fats and oils are lipids; many are triglycerides.
A triglyceride consists of one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acid molecules.
The fatty acids may be saturated or unsaturated, which affects the properties of the fat or oil.
Lipids store energy in their chemical bonds and can be broken down to release it when required.
They form a compact, long-term energy reserve and store more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

written.text: Q6.5. Explain the double helix structure of DNA, and discuss the base pairing in this structure.
written.finalAnswer: DNA consists of two antiparallel nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. The bases pair specifically: adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine.

rubric.why: The double helix consists of two strands.
rubric.description: Describe the overall shape and number of strands.
rubric.how: State that DNA has two strands twisted into a double helix.

rubric.why: The backbone forms the outside of each strand.
rubric.how: Name the sugar-phosphate backbone.

rubric.why: DNA is built from nucleotides, each carrying a base.
rubric.description: Identify the building units and bases.
rubric.how: State that DNA strands are made of nucleotides with nitrogenous bases.

rubric.why: The A–T complementary pair must be correct.
rubric.how: State that adenine pairs with thymine.

rubric.why: The C–G complementary pair must be correct.
rubric.how: State that cytosine pairs with guanine.

modelAnswer: DNA is made of two long nucleotide strands twisted around one another to form a double helix.
Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and nitrogenous bases directed towards the inside.
The bases on the two strands pair specifically by hydrogen bonds.
Adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T).
Cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G).

written.text: Q6.6. Explain how the information in DNA is converted to RNA and then to proteins.
written.finalAnswer: DNA information is transcribed into mRNA; the mRNA is translated at a ribosome, where tRNA brings amino acids that are joined to form a protein.

rubric.why: The process begins with genetic information in DNA.
rubric.how: State that a DNA gene contains the instructions.

rubric.why: Transcription makes an RNA copy of the DNA information.
rubric.how: State that the DNA code is transcribed into mRNA.

rubric.why: Translation takes place at the ribosome.
rubric.how: Mention a ribosome and translation.

rubric.why: The ribosome reads the mRNA code in units to determine the amino acid order.
rubric.description: Explain how the code is read.
rubric.how: Mention codons or reading the mRNA sequence.

rubric.why: The amino acids are assembled in the order specified to make a protein.
rubric.how: State that tRNA brings amino acids which are linked into a polypeptide/protein.

modelAnswer: A gene is a section of DNA that contains instructions for making a protein.
During transcription, a complementary mRNA copy of the information is made.
The mRNA moves to a ribosome, where its bases are read in groups called codons.
During translation, tRNA molecules bring amino acids matching the mRNA code.
The amino acids are joined in the correct order to form a polypeptide, which folds into a protein.

written.text: Q6.1. Evaluate the importance of water in the functioning of biomolecules.
written.finalAnswer: Water is a solvent and reaction medium, helps transport substances, participates in reactions and helps maintain cell conditions; therefore it is essential for biomolecule function.

rubric.why: Many biomolecules and substances need water as a solvent.
rubric.how: State that water dissolves many substances.

rubric.why: Cell reactions occur in an aqueous environment and some use water directly.
rubric.how: Mention reaction medium or water participating in reactions.

rubric.why: Dissolved substances can be transported in water.
rubric.how: Mention transport of nutrients, wastes or other substances.

rubric.why: The answer should evaluate why water matters to normal cell function.
rubric.description: Give an overall conclusion or another valid role.
rubric.how: Conclude that water is essential, or mention temperature regulation or maintaining biomolecule function.

modelAnswer: Water is a good solvent, so many biomolecules and ions dissolve in it.
It provides the medium in which many cellular reactions occur; water is also used or produced in some reactions.
Water carries dissolved nutrients and wastes through organisms and cells.
It helps maintain suitable conditions, including temperature, for biomolecules to work.
Therefore, without water, many biomolecular reactions and life processes could not function properly.

written.text: Q6.2. Find the amount/ percentage of carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats and water in the following food product and compare them with each other:  Roti(40gm), Burger, Cucumber, Egg, Rice(100gm), Potato fries(100gm),Carrot
written.finalAnswer: Approximate values vary by recipe and preparation; see the table in the model answer. Roti and rice are highest in carbohydrate, egg is highest in protein among the listed plain foods, potato fries are high in fat, and cucumber and carrot contain a high proportion of water.

rubric.why: The comparison must include the specified 40 g roti.
rubric.description: Report an approximate value for roti.
rubric.how: Give its approximate carbohydrate, protein, fat and water values.

rubric.why: The first comparison group must be represented.
rubric.description: Report values for burger, cucumber and egg.
rubric.how: Include approximate nutrient information for these foods.

rubric.why: The remaining listed foods must be included.
rubric.description: Report values for rice, fries and carrot.
rubric.how: Include approximate nutrient information for all three.

rubric.why: The question asks for amounts or percentages of all four components.
rubric.description: Use comparable amounts and identify the components.
rubric.how: Give carbohydrate, protein, fat and water per 100 g, or clearly state the serving basis.

rubric.why: The question explicitly asks for a comparison, and food composition varies.
rubric.description: Compare the foods and indicate the values are approximate.
rubric.how: State the main high/low patterns and note recipe or preparation variation.

modelAnswer: Approximate composition per 100 g of edible food; values vary with recipe, brand and cooking method. Roti is shown for the stated 40 g serving.
Food | carbohydrate (g) | protein (g) | fat (g) | water (g)
Roti, 40 g | about 22 | about 3.5 | about 1.2 | about 12
Burger, typical prepared burger, 100 g | about 25 | about 12 | about 12 | about 48
Cucumber, 100 g | about 3.6 | about 0.7 | about 0.1 | about 95
Egg, 100 g | about 0.7 | about 13 | about 11 | about 76
Rice, cooked, 100 g | about 28 | about 2.7 | about 0.3 | about 68
Potato fries, 100 g | about 41 | about 3.4 | about 15 | about 40
Carrot, 100 g | about 9.6 | about 0.9 | about 0.2 | about 88
Roti and cooked rice are rich in carbohydrates compared with their protein and fat.
Egg has more protein than cucumber, carrot and cooked rice per 100 g; a burger's protein depends on its ingredients.
Potato fries have much more fat than plain cucumber, carrot or cooked rice.
Cucumber and carrot have high water content; the exact burger and fries values vary considerably with preparation.

examTips: Short questions commonly ask for definitions, examples, functions or the components of a molecule; answer directly and include the key terms.
For structure questions, label the important parts clearly: amino group, carboxyl group and R group for an amino acid; glycerol and three fatty acids for a fat.
Long answers often ask for a comparison or a process. Organise the answer into clear points and give examples such as starch, haemoglobin or antibodies.
For DNA base pairing, write both pairs exactly: A–T and C–G. For protein synthesis, distinguish transcription from translation.
For food-composition questions, state the serving size and units, and note that values can vary with recipe and cooking method.

steps.text: DNA is made of two long nucleotide strands twisted around one another to form a double helix.

steps.why: The backbone and bases describe how each strand is arranged.
steps.text: Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and nitrogenous bases directed towards the inside.

example.question: Q6.5. Explain the double helix structure of DNA, and discuss the base pairing in this structure.
example.answer: DNA consists of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and bases on the inside. Adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine.

explain.title: Carbohydrates
explain.body: Monosaccharides are single sugar units; disaccharides have two joined sugar units; polysaccharides have many. Carbohydrates provide energy, store energy and can build structures such as plant cell walls.

explain.title: Proteins
explain.body: Proteins are made from amino acids. Their functions include structure, growth and repair, enzyme action, transport, defence, movement and blood clotting.

explain.title: Lipids
explain.body: Many fats and oils are triglycerides made from glycerol and three fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.

explain.title: Nucleic acids
explain.body: DNA stores genetic information. Its two strands form a double helix with complementary base pairs A–T and C–G. RNA includes mRNA, tRNA and rRNA and helps make proteins.

explain.title: Water and food
explain.body: Water dissolves and transports substances and provides a medium for cellular reactions. Food nutrient values are estimates and can change with serving size, ingredients and cooking.

mistakes: Do not confuse a single sugar (monosaccharide) with a many-unit polysaccharide.
Do not say humans digest cellulose; it provides structural support in plants and is dietary fibre for humans.
Do not confuse the roles of proteins: haemoglobin transports oxygen, antibodies defend against pathogens, and enzymes help reactions.
Do not describe unsaturated fatty acids as having no double bonds; that describes saturated fatty acids.
Do not swap DNA base pairs: adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine.
When drawing structures, include all required parts and labels; a list of names alone may not earn the drawing marks.
For nutrition comparisons, do not compare values on different serving-size bases without converting them.
